# GitHub {#github background-color="#f0674d"}

A safe copy of your project in the cloud, if you want one.

## git and GitHub

```{=html}
{{< include images/git-branches.svg >}}
```

> OneDrive keeps your files in sync. GitHub keeps every version, and who changed what.

## Why a researcher might want it

- **Backup with history.** Not `final_v3_REALLY_final.docx`.
- **Co-authors on one folder.** No more emailing files back and forth.
- **Replication packages.** Journals increasingly ask for code and data. A GitHub
  repository, archived on Zenodo, gets a DOI you can cite.
- **Course pages.** Plain text in, a web page out, updated with every push.

## Set up, once

1. Make a free account at **github.com**. Private repositories are free.
2. Then ask the agent:

::: {.prompt}
Install the GitHub command-line tool and log me in.
:::

It installs `gh` and opens your browser to log in. Approve, and you're done.

## Put a folder on GitHub

::: {.prompt}
Put this folder on GitHub as a private repository called [name]. Check .gitignore
first: no PDFs, no raw data, nothing confidential.
:::

After that, whenever you've committed something worth keeping:

::: {.prompt}
Push my latest changes.
:::

**Laptop dead?** On the new one: *"Download my repository [name] into this
folder."* Everything is back, with its whole history.

## Working with a co-author

- You: *"Add [their GitHub username] as a collaborator."*
- They: *"Download [the repository link] into this folder."*
- Every session: *"Pull the latest changes."* Work. *"Commit and push."*
- Both edited the same file? *"Merge our changes and show me what you did."*

Or they **propose** changes instead of pushing them. That's a pull request.

## Pull requests: propose, don't push {#pr}

```{=html}
{{< include images/pr-flow.svg >}}
```

Nothing lands in your project until you say **merge**. The discussion stays attached
to the change. *It's referee-and-revise, for a folder.*

## Live: Jonas and Ludvik {#demo}

1. **Jonas** puts a folder on GitHub and adds Ludvik.
2. **Ludvik** downloads it, makes a change on a branch, and opens a pull request.
3. **Jonas** reads it, tests it, and comments.
4. **Ludvik** fixes it. **Jonas** merges.

Neither of us types a git command. The prompts are on the next two slides.

## Their side

::: {.prompt}
Make a new branch, [the change], commit it, push it, and open a pull request to
[owner] that explains what you changed and why.
:::

The agent makes the branch, writes the description and opens the pull request.
They never see a git command.

## Your side

::: {.prompt}
Are there open pull requests on this repository? Summarise them.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Check out the pull request and test it. Does everything still run? Do any numbers change?
:::

Then one of:

- *"Comment on the pull request: [your question]."*
- *"Merge it, then pull the latest changes."*

## Exercise: in pairs {#pairs}

Both: a GitHub account, and *"Install the GitHub command-line tool and log me in."*

1. **A:** *"Put this folder on GitHub as a private repository called [name], and add
   [B's username] as a collaborator."*
2. **B:** *"Accept the GitHub invitation from [A's username], and download
   [A's username]/[name] into this folder."*
3. **B:** *"Make a new branch, [your change], and open a pull request that explains it."*
4. **A:** *"Any open pull requests? Summarise them."* Comment, or merge. Then swap.

## Keep an eye on it

- **GitHub tells you.** *Watch* the repository: an email, or a push notification
  in the GitHub app, for every new pull request.
- **Claude Code, while it's open,** can check on a timer:

::: {.prompt}
/loop 10m check for new pull requests on this repository, and summarise any new ones.
:::

- **A reviewer on GitHub itself.** Connect the Claude or Codex app to the
  repository once. Then a comment with `@claude` or `@codex review` on a pull
  request gets you a review.

## Public or private

- **Private by default.** Only you and the people you invite can see it.
- **Public** only for things you'd publish anyway: a replication package, a course page.
- **History is forever.** A file you "delete" later is still in the history. So
  never commit passwords, student data or confidential data in the first place.
- Research data: check the data agreement before it goes to any cloud service.
